analysis.one_liner: Bans data brokers from selling people's location and health information.
analysis.headline: Introduced in December 2024 with four Senate sponsors, the bill never got a hearing or a vote before Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would make it illegal for data brokers — companies that collect and resell information about people — to sell, license, or share anyone's location data or health data. That includes data revealing a pregnancy, a miscarriage, a mental health condition, a disability, or a person's physical movements. The Federal Trade Commission would write the rules and enforce the ban, with states' attorneys general and private individuals also allowed to sue violators. Companies breaking the law could face fines of up to 15 percent of their parent company's annual revenue.
analysis.who_benefits: Anyone whose phone or app use generates location or health signals — which is nearly everyone. The bill would stop brokers from selling records of visits to clinics, pregnancy apps, mental health searches, and location trails to advertisers, insurers, employers, or others. It gives the FTC $1 billion to do the enforcement work and lets state attorneys general and individuals sue.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Anyone with a smartphone or health app

how_it_helps.text: Prohibits data brokers from selling, reselling, licensing, trading, or transferring any individual's location data or health data, including inferred data. [S2]

Defines health data broadly to include searches for health services, pregnancy and miscarriage, mental health conditions, and disabilities, so the ban reaches data people never knowingly handed over. [S2]

Enforces the ban through the FTC, state attorneys general, and a private right of action, with civil penalties up to 15 percent of the violator's ultimate parent entity's annual revenue and deletion of the affected data. [S2]
Appropriates $1 billion to the FTC to fund rulemaking and enforcement. [S2]

Keeps protections narrow but real: HIPAA-compliant handling, newsworthy publication, and disclosures the individual validly authorized are exempted, and state laws are preempted only where they require the prohibited disclosure. [S2]

analysis.who_pays: Data brokers and the app and advertising companies that buy their data would lose a market built on selling sensitive information. Some firms would bear compliance and litigation costs, and private lawsuits could impose costs beyond the worst-behaved firms.
analysis.who_pays_short: Data brokers and digital ad firms

drawbacks.text: The penalty is capped at 15 percent of the parent company's prior-year revenue, and appeals all route through the D.C. Circuit, which concentrates enforcement in a single court and could limit deterrence for large firms. [S2]

A private right of action with attorney's fees could generate litigation against firms whose practices are near the line, and the FTC has only 180 days to write rules defining key terms like 'data,' raising the risk of contested, shifting standards. [S2]

Because the ban covers data 'linked or reasonably linkable' to groups as well as individuals, some legitimate research, analytics, and journalism could face compliance burdens, though the bill exempts newsworthy publication and validly authorized disclosures. [S2]

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core protection is strong and directly aimed at a market most people do not know exists: the resale of their movements and health signals. The design has real flaws — a revenue-capped penalty, D.C.-only appellate jurisdiction, and a rushed rulemaking clock — but the costs fall mainly on firms profiting from sensitive data resale, and the bill preserves normal medical handling, journalism, and authorized sharing. The benefit to ordinary people outweighs the drawbacks, though the penalty cap may underdeter the largest firms.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in the Senate and referred to the Commerce Committee, which never took it up before the two-year Congress ended, so it died with no hearing and no vote.

narrative.text: Senator Elizabeth Warren introduced the bill on December 10, 2024, with Senators Sanders, Whitehouse, and Wyden as original cosponsors. [S2]
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation, and no further action was ever recorded. [S4]
The bill's only cosponsors beyond its sponsor were three senators: 2 of 48 Senate Democrats and 1 of 4 independents who caucus with Democrats; no Republican sponsored or cosponsored it. [S3]
The Congress ended on January 3, 2025, and the bill expired without leaving committee. [S1]

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Data brokers and the app and advertising companies that buy location and health data are better off, because the sale of that data remains legal and unregulated at the federal level.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Data brokers and their data buyers

for.name: Sen. Elizabeth Warren
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Health and Location Data Protection Act of 2024 in the Senate.

for.name: Sens. Sanders, Whitehouse, and Wyden
for.role: 2 of 48 Senate Democrats and 1 of 4 Senate independents (cosponsors)
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill at introduction; no other senators joined.

against.name: Senate Commerce, Science, and Transportation Committee
against.role: Committee of referral, chaired by Sen. Maria Cantwell (D-WA)
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on December 10, 2024, and took no recorded action — no hearing, no markup, no vote — for the remainder of the Congress.

against.name: Senate Republican conference
against.what_they_did: No Republican sponsored or cosponsored the bill, leaving it without the cross-party support typically needed to move in the Senate.

sides.party_line_note: There was no vote to measure partisanship, but the bill's four sponsors were all Democrats or allied independents and no Republican joined, suggesting a partisan split on a privacy bill that drew no floor test.

industries.note: These companies' core business is collecting and reselling information, including health and location data the bill defines; the ban would cut off their most sensitive product lines. Ordinary people currently have no practical way to stop or even see these sales.

Ad networks and app developers buy broker data and location signals to target people; the ban would remove a cheap targeting input. Consumers currently pay for 'free' apps partly with this data trail.

Firms that infer health conditions from browsing or purchases would lose the resale market, but HIPAA-compliant handling and validly authorized disclosure remain permitted, so compliant firms keep operating.
